title: Distributions, Sampling & the Central Limit Theorem
excerpt: A distribution shows the values data can take; a sampling distribution shows how a summary such as an average would vary across samples. Explore why averages often become more stable, and where small samples, dependence and changing conditions make simple rules unreliable.
objectives: Distinguish a population distribution, sample, statistic and sampling distribution.
Explain the law of large numbers and central limit theorem in plain English, including their assumptions.
Calculate and interpret standard error and a simple confidence interval for a mean in financial units.
Use bootstrap intuition while respecting dependence, heavy tails, changing regimes and selection in time-series data.

lessons.title: Four distributions hiding in one finance question
lessons.body:
A population distribution describes every unit in the target group, such as all daily returns in a defined market and period. A sample is the observed subset; a statistic is a number computed from it, such as the sample mean. A sampling distribution is the pattern of that statistic across repeated samples from the population. These are different objects. If five illustrative daily returns are −2%, 1%, 0%, 3% and −1%, their sample mean is (−2 + 1 + 0 + 3 − 1)% ÷ 5 = 0.2% per day. That single 0.2% is not the population mean and says nothing about causality. Keep the unit, sampling frame and time window visible.

A useful way to separate the four objects is to track a question about hourly wages. Suppose a firm’s target population is all 2,000 employees, measured in dollars per hour during March 2026 (illustrative synthetic data). A randomly selected sample of 50 employees is the observed subset. If their wages sum to $1,250 per hour, the sample statistic is x̄ = $1,250 ÷ 50 = $25 per hour. Now imagine repeating that selection many times: the resulting list of sample means is a sampling distribution, also measured in dollars per hour. The population distribution contains individual wages, not sample means. A sample mean estimates a population mean but can differ because of selection noise. It does not describe wage causation or guarantee representativeness. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Sampling Distributions” in the linked sources.

Suppose an analyst wants the average daily return over a 25-day window, and use the following numbers only as an illustrative synthetic calculation: an assumed daily standard deviation of 1.5 percentage points and a sample mean of 0.42 percentage points per day. The standard error of the mean is σ/√n = 1.5/√25 = 1.5/5 = 0.30 percentage points per day. If the reference value is 0.30 percentage points per day, the standardized distance is (0.42 − 0.30)/0.30 = 0.40, so the estimate is less than half a standard error above that reference. A normal-approximation 95% reference interval is 0.42 ± 1.96(0.30), or −0.168 to 1.008 percentage points per day (rounding to −0.17 to 1.01). The interval includes the reference and even negative average returns, so this calculation does not establish a reliably positive economic result. It also requires that the 25 observations be sufficiently independent and drawn from a stable process; volatility clustering or a regime shift can make 1.5/√25 too optimistic. In the CLT lab, increasing repeated samples makes the histogram smoother, whereas increasing n is what changes the spread of the simulated means.
lessons.takeaway: The raw-return distribution and the sampling distribution of an average answer different questions.

practice.question: In the five-return example, what is the statistic and what would a sampling distribution contain?
practice.hint: The statistic is calculated once from the observed sample; repeat the sampling process conceptually.
practice.solution: The statistic is x̄ = 0.2% per day. A sampling distribution would contain many means, each calculated from a new sample of five returns under the same sampling design.

lessons.title: The law of large numbers: stability, not certainty
lessons.body:
The law of large numbers says that, under a stable data-generating process and suitable sampling conditions, an average tends to move toward the population mean as n, the number of observations, grows. It does not say every next return will be near the mean, nor does it repair a biased sample. For an illustrative sequence of daily returns 1%, −1%, 2% and 0%, the running means are 1%, 0%, 0.67% and 0.50%. The path wanders while the average becomes less sensitive to one additional observation. In finance, changing volatility, dependence, structural breaks and heavy tails can weaken this shortcut, so state assumptions rather than promise convergence on a deadline.

The law of large numbers concerns the cumulative average, not a promise about each observation. Imagine illustrative synthetic hourly exchange-rate changes of +2%, −1%, +3%, −2%, and +1%. After two observations, the mean is (2 − 1)% ÷ 2 = 0.5% per hour; after five, it is (2 − 1 + 3 − 2 + 1)% ÷ 5 = 0.6% per hour. Adding one new observation can still move the average substantially when n is small. With a stable population and an appropriate sampling process, additional observations tend to reduce this random movement. The result does not remove a systematic sampling bias, serial dependence, or a regime change, and it does not say the next hourly change will be near 0.6%. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 4: Distributions (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.

Track a running average in the unit that matters, but keep it separate from a forecast. Suppose, illustratively, that six synthetic quarterly real-wage growth rates (percentage points per quarter) are 1.2, −0.4, 0.8, 1.6, −0.2, and 0.5. Their sum is 3.5 pp, so the six-quarter average is 3.5 ÷ 6 = 0.583 pp per quarter. A second synthetic block, 0.7, −0.1, 1.1, −0.3, 0.4, and 0.2, sums to 2.0 pp and averages 0.333 pp per quarter; combining all twelve gives (3.5 + 2.0) ÷ 12 = 0.458 pp per quarter. That combined average is nearer to an illustrative long-run mean of 0.5 pp per quarter than the first block, but improvement is not guaranteed at every step. Before invoking the law of large numbers, check that quarters are comparably defined, selected without outcome-based filtering, and plausibly stable; a policy break or serial dependence can make more observations precise about a changing mixture rather than closer to one fixed mean. This running average differs from the lab’s generated repeated sample means, although both summarize averages.
lessons.takeaway: More observations can reduce random averaging noise, but not bias, regime change or tail risk.

lessons.title: What the central limit theorem actually says
lessons.body:
The central limit theorem (CLT) says that, for many averages, the sampling distribution of x̄ becomes approximately normal as n becomes sufficiently large, when observations are suitably independent or dependence is handled and variance is well behaved. It does not make individual returns normal. Suppose daily returns have population mean μ = 0.10% and standard deviation σ = 2.0% under an illustrative independent model. For n = 100 days, the standard error is σ/√n = 2.0%/10 = 0.20% per day. A mean of 0.55% is 0.45 percentage points above μ, or 2.25 standard errors. That standardized distance describes sampling evidence under the model, not a causal effect or forecast.

Keep two pictures separate: the spread of individual observations and the spread of averages from repeated samples. For a teaching example, suppose household weekly energy bills have a standard deviation of about £200. A random sample of 100 households has a standard error for its average of roughly £200 ÷ √100 = £20. If we repeatedly took new samples of 100 from the same population, their averages would vary around the true average; they would not all equal it. With 400 independent households, the standard error would be about £200 ÷ √400 = £10.

The central limit theorem helps explain why that repeated-sample distribution of averages can look approximately bell-shaped under suitable conditions. It does not say that individual bills become bell-shaped, nor that a large sample repairs a biased survey. The shortcut relies on an appropriate sampling process and enough effectively independent information; strong clustering, serial dependence, very heavy tails or a changing population can alter the approximation. See the Penn State STAT 200 notes on Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem linked below.

The CLT is especially useful when the raw observations are uneven but the average combines enough suitable observations. In an illustrative synthetic model, weekly claims have mean $300 and standard deviation $80 per household-week. For n = 16 independent households, SE(x̄) ≈ $80 ÷ √16 = $80 ÷ 4 = $20 per household-week. For n = 64, SE(x̄) ≈ $80 ÷ 8 = $10 per household-week, so the typical sampling spread halves when the sample quadruples. This describes repeated sample averages, not individual claims becoming normal; a particular sample can still be unusual. Independence, a stable population, and finite, well-behaved variance matter. Clustering households or extreme tails can make the simple calculation too optimistic. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Central Limit Theorem” in the linked sources.

Here is a dependence check that the lab’s independent simulation does not perform. Suppose, purely illustratively, that 25 consecutive daily returns have a sample standard deviation of 1.5 percentage points and lag-one autocorrelation ρ = 0.40. The independent-observation shortcut would give SE(x̄) = 1.5/√25 = 0.30 percentage points per day. For a roughly stationary AR(1)-type dependence pattern, a large-n approximation is an effective sample size n_eff ≈ n(1−ρ)/(1+ρ), so n_eff ≈ 25(0.60)/(1.40) = 10.71. The dependence-adjusted SE is therefore about 1.5/√10.71 = 0.46 percentage points per day, roughly 53% larger than 0.30 (0.16/0.30 ≈ 0.53). The arithmetic is illustrative, not an estimate from observed returns. This adjustment assumes a stable autocorrelation structure and finite variance; volatility clustering, changing regimes, or higher-order autocorrelation can invalidate the simple formula. Thus, when interpreting repeated means, ask whether the simulated or observed observations supply 25 independent pieces of information before treating the CLT spread as a precision claim.
lessons.takeaway: The CLT concerns a statistic across repeated samples, and its approximation depends on data conditions.

practice.question: If the same model used n = 400 days instead, what happens to the standard error?
practice.solution: SE(x̄) ≈ 2.0%/20 = 0.10% per day, half the n = 100 standard error. This is a reduction in sampling uncertainty, not a guarantee that returns are less volatile.

lessons.title: Standard error and an interval in percentage points
lessons.body:
A standard error summarizes typical sample-to-sample variation in an estimator, not the standard deviation of individual returns. Consider 64 illustrative, approximately independent monthly returns with sample mean x̄ = 0.8% per month and sample standard deviation s = 4.0% per month. Estimate the mean's standard error as s/√n = 4.0%/8 = 0.5 percentage points per month. Using a rough 95% multiplier of 2 gives x̄ ± 2SE = 0.8% ± 1.0%, or (−0.2%, 1.8%) per month. Under the sampling assumptions, the procedure has about 95% long-run coverage. This is not a probability that this fixed interval contains the parameter, and it is not a next-month forecast.

Illustrative synthetic example — A regional labour economist estimates the mean district-level unemployment rate in April 2026 from a simple random sample of 64 districts. The sample mean is 6.0%, and the sample standard deviation across districts is 1.6 percentage points. First estimate the standard error of the mean: 1.6 ÷ √64 = 1.6 ÷ 8 = 0.2 percentage points. Using a rough 95% multiplier of 2 gives 6.0% ± 2(0.2 percentage points), or an interval from 5.6% to 6.4%. In this teaching calculation, 6.0% is the sample estimate; the interval expresses sampling uncertainty about the region’s April mean district rate under the stated design, not the rate in any one district or a forecast for May.

The interval method can quantify sampling uncertainty for the stated district-level average, but it cannot repair nonresponse, a biased district list, measurement errors, or a change in labour-market conditions after April; it also does not establish that a policy caused unemployment to change. Check that the 64 districts were sampled in a defensible way, that rates use consistent definitions, and whether spatial clustering or other dependence makes 64 observations fewer than 64 independent pieces of information. Avoid saying there is a 95% probability that this fixed interval contains the mean: the approximately 95% claim belongs to the long-run procedure when its assumptions hold. For the formal sampling-distribution logic, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Sampling Distributions” in the linked sources below.

Standard error is measured in the same units as the estimate, while a percentage-point interval should not be confused with a percent change. Suppose an illustrative synthetic survey of n = 25 stores finds a mean monthly revenue growth of 4% and sample standard deviation 5 percentage points. The estimated standard error is 5 ÷ √25 = 5 ÷ 5 = 1 percentage point per month. A rough 95% interval is 4% ± 2(1 percentage point), giving 2% to 6% monthly growth. The half-width is 2 percentage points, not “2 percent of 4%.” This interval describes uncertainty in the population mean monthly growth under the sampling design; it is not a forecast for next month. Nonresponse, dependence among stores, or changing conditions can invalidate the coverage claim. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 200 — Sampling Distributions” in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic planning example — Suppose an analyst wants to estimate a portfolio’s mean daily return with a rough 95% margin of error no wider than 0.6 percentage points. A pilot simulation, not observed market data, suggests a daily-return standard deviation of 3.0 percentage points. Using the rough critical value of 2, solve the standard-error requirement before collecting the main sample: 2s/√n ≤ 0.6, so n ≥ (2 × 3.0 ÷ 0.6)² = 10² = 100 trading days. With n = 100, the estimated SE is 3.0 ÷ √100 = 0.30 percentage points per day, and the half-width is 2 × 0.30 = 0.60 percentage points; a mean of 0.20% per day would therefore give the illustrative interval −0.40% to 0.80% per day. The planning result is conditional on roughly independent, similarly distributed days and a useful volatility estimate. Volatility clustering, serial dependence, heavy tails, or a regime shift can make uncertainty larger, so increasing n is not a guarantee of representative evidence; block methods or a dependence-aware model may be preferable. The target is precision for a mean, not a forecast or causal claim.
lessons.takeaway: Intervals express uncertainty about an estimand; they do not turn historical averages into predictions.

practice.question: What does the interval (−0.2%, 1.8%) say about a zero monthly mean?
practice.hint: Check whether zero lies between the endpoints, then distinguish compatibility from proof.
practice.solution: Zero lies inside the interval, so a zero mean is compatible with this rough procedure and sample. That does not prove the mean is zero, and it does not address causality or practical importance.

lessons.title: Bootstrap the statistic, not the story
lessons.body:
A basic bootstrap repeatedly samples the observed values with replacement, recomputes a statistic, and uses the resulting distribution to approximate sampling variability. For an illustrative sample of five daily returns, one bootstrap replicate might resample −2%, −2%, 0%, 1%, and 3%; its mean is (−2 − 2 + 0 + 1 + 3)% ÷ 5 = 0%. Thousands of such replicates show how the mean might vary if this sample represents the target process. The bootstrap cannot create unseen crashes, correct survivorship bias or establish causality. Percentile intervals can be useful when the bootstrap distribution is skewed, but the method remains conditional on the original data and design.

Bootstrap calculation is transparent when each resample keeps the original sample size and allows repeats. Take an illustrative synthetic sample of four delivery times in minutes: 20, 30, 40, and 50. One bootstrap resample could be 20, 20, 40, 50, whose mean is (20 + 20 + 40 + 50) ÷ 4 = 32.5 minutes. Another could be 30, 30, 50, 50, with mean 40 minutes. Repeating this many times gives a distribution of bootstrap means; its spread approximates uncertainty about the original sample mean, in minutes. It is conditional on the observed four times: an unobserved 90-minute disruption cannot appear unless represented in the data. Ordinary resampling also assumes exchangeable observations, so daily dependence or changing traffic regimes requires caution. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 4: Distributions (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.

For a median, the resampled statistic changes through order rather than through an arithmetic average. Suppose an explicitly synthetic sample of seven monthly grocery-price changes is 1.0%, 1.4%, 1.8%, 2.1%, 3.0%, 4.5%, and 7.2%; the observed median is the fourth ordered value, 2.1% per month. One bootstrap draw must still contain seven observations, but may repeat values: 1.0%, 1.8%, 1.8%, 3.0%, 4.5%, 7.2%, 7.2%. After sorting, its median is 3.0% per month (the fourth value). Repeat this resampling B times, store all B medians, and sort those results. The bootstrap standard error is the sample standard deviation of those medians; a percentile interval uses, for example, the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the stored values, retaining percentage-point units. This interval describes uncertainty under the observed sample’s empirical distribution, not a probability that the fixed population median lies inside it. With only seven observations, one unusual month can be copied often, and a time-ordered series may require block resampling rather than ordinary independent draws.
lessons.takeaway: Resampling quantifies uncertainty under the observed sample; it does not manufacture new evidence.

lessons.title: From a distribution to a responsible conclusion
lessons.body:
A distribution can reveal association, uncertainty and unusual observations, but it cannot by itself identify a cause. Imagine a simulated 10-year index-return sample: a 60-day block-mean histogram looks more bell-shaped than the daily-return histogram, while a few daily losses remain extreme. That supports a statement about sampling behavior under the simulation, not a claim that a policy caused returns or that the mean predicts the next block. Distinguish statistical evidence from practical importance: a tiny mean can be precisely estimated in a huge sample, while a costly tail event can remain uncertain. Report units, sample construction, dependence checks and limitations before making a decision.

A responsible conclusion links the statistic to a clearly stated estimand and avoids jumping from association to cause. Suppose an illustrative synthetic comparison finds average annual returns of 6% for Fund A and 4% for Fund B over 10 years: the arithmetic difference is 6% − 4% = 2 percentage points per year. That comparison does not show Fund A caused the extra return; sector mix, fees, risk, and selection may differ. Nor does a 2-percentage-point average establish that every future year will be better. Report the observation period, currency or return unit, sample construction, uncertainty, and tail behavior. Practical importance also matters: a 2-point gain may be outweighed by a 10-point loss in a rare year. For a fuller treatment, see “MIT OpenCourseWare — Random Walks and Financial Data” in the linked sources.

To turn the lab’s moving histogram into a decision quantity, suppose an explicitly synthetic teaching sample has a mean daily return of 0.8 percentage points, a sample standard deviation of 3.5 percentage points, and n = 25 independent trading-day observations. The estimated standard error of the mean is s/√n = 3.5/√25 = 3.5/5 = 0.7 percentage points per day. A rough 95% reference interval is therefore 0.8 ± 1.96(0.7), giving 0.8 ± 1.372, or −0.572 to 2.172 percentage points per day (about −0.57 to 2.17 pp/day). The interval crosses zero, so this small synthetic sample does not distinguish a positive average from no average daily change at that reference level. It also does not say that 95% of future daily returns lie inside the interval: the interval concerns the unknown mean, not individual outcomes. Before using the shortcut, check whether observations are plausibly independent and whether extreme tails or volatility clustering make s unstable; dependence reduces the effective information, while a regime shift can make this historical uncertainty unrepresentative. These numbers are illustrative, not observed returns or an investment forecast.
lessons.takeaway: Describe what the data support, then label prediction, causality, uncertainty and practical importance separately.

caseStudy: Consider a deliberately illustrative exercise using simulated daily returns for a broad index, not an invented historical dataset. Generate 10,000 draws from a heavy-tailed distribution with a mean of 0.04% per day, then form 1,000 non-overlapping blocks of 60 observations and calculate each block mean. First plot the daily returns: the center may be tight while the tails contain unusually large gains and losses. Next plot the 60-day means: averaging often makes the center look more regular, but the spread depends on the return variance and any dependence across days. Compare the empirical standard deviation of block means with the shortcut σ/√60. If volatility clusters or the simulation changes regime, the shortcut can understate uncertainty. A bootstrap from one observed sample will also miss regimes not represented there, and an ordinary bootstrap breaks time dependence. The exercise demonstrates sampling distributions and approximation limits; it does not forecast performance, establish that any market event caused a return, or justify an investment. A responsible report would state the simulated nature, distributional assumptions, block construction, units, uncertainty method and practical decision threshold.
misconceptions: The CLT says individual returns become normally distributed as n grows. It concerns the sampling distribution of a statistic such as a mean.
A larger sample guarantees a close or representative estimate. It can reduce random error while leaving selection bias, dependence, regime change and heavy tails.
A bootstrap sample is new independent evidence. It reuses the observed data and cannot recover missing regimes or repair a biased design.
A narrow interval or statistically detectable pattern proves causation or practical importance. Precision, association, causal identification and economic value are distinct questions.
A non-significant or wide result proves there is no effect. It may reflect limited information, high variability or a poorly powered design.

quiz.question: What does the central limit theorem describe in its common use for sample means?
options: The raw data become normally distributed.
The sampling distribution of many sample means can be approximately normal under suitable conditions.
Every sample mean equals the population mean.
quiz.explanation: The theorem is about the repeated-sample distribution of a statistic, not a guarantee about any one sample or the shape of raw returns.
